rpName
is the human-readable name of your app. Users will see it in the operating system's passkey prompt and later in their password manager.

Generate Registration Options

The first method finds or creates the user, then asks SimpleWebAuthn for registration options. Add it inside the class:

async generateRegistrationOptions(
    email: string,
): Promise {
  let user = await this.userRepository.findOne({ where: { email } });

  if (!user) {
    user = this.userRepository.create({
      email,
      webauthnId: randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'),
    });
    await this.userRepository.save(user);
  }

  const authenticators = await this.authenticatorRepository.find({
    where: { user: { id: user.id } },
  });

  if (authenticators.length > 0) {
    throw new ConflictException(
      'An account with this email already exists. Please sign in.',
    );
  }

  const options = await generateRegistrationOptions({
    rpName: this.rpName,
    rpID: this.rpID,
    userID: Buffer.from(user.webauthnId, 'base64url'),
    userName: user.email,
    attestationType: 'none',
    authenticatorSelection: {
      residentKey: 'required',
      userVerification: 'required',
    },
    excludeCredentials: authenticators.map((authenticator) => ({
      id: authenticator.credentialId,
      transports: authenticator.transports,
    })),
  });

  // Save the current challenge
  user.currentChallenge = options.challenge;
  await this.userRepository.save(user);

  return options;
}

The 

authenticatorSelection
block is where you decide what kind of passkey you want.

residentKey: 'required'
asks for a discoverable credential. That's what makes it a true passkey (the credential is stored on the device or in the user's password manager and can then sync to their other devices).

userVerification: 'required'
tells the device that it needs to verify the user (that is, check their fingerprint, face, or screen lock). Without that, some of the authenticators would just do a presence check and not actually verify the user.

What's missing is an authenticator attachment option. If you set it to 

'platform'
, that would effectively lock users into using the sensor on their current device. If you leave it out, then they can use their phone via QR code or a hardware security key (which is what passkeys.dev recommends).

attestationType: 'none'
means you're not asking the device to attest to its make and model. Most consumer apps don't need that at all, and asking for it can in fact trigger additional privacy prompts.

excludeCredentials
lists the passkeys the user already has so the device won't create a duplicate on an authenticator that's already registered. Given the check immediately above it, that list is always empty in this case. It becomes useful later on when you allow signed-in users to add further passkeys.

The check for existing authenticators is also important. This endpoint doesn't require the user to be signed in, so you can't just allow it to add a passkey to an account that already has one. Otherwise, anyone who knows your email address could attach their own passkey to your account.

Verify the Registration Response

After the user confirms on their device, the browser sends back a response. The second method verifies it and stores the new passkey:

async verifyRegistration(email: string, response: RegistrationResponseJSON) {
  const user = await this.userRepository.findOne({
    where: { email },
    select: ['id', 'email', 'currentChallenge', 'webauthnId'],
  });

  if (!user) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException('User not found');
  }

  const verification = await verifyRegistrationResponse({
    response,
    expectedChallenge: user.currentChallenge,
    expectedOrigin: this.origin,
    expectedRPID: this.rpID,
    requireUserVerification: true,
  });

  const { verified, registrationInfo } = verification;

  if (verified && registrationInfo) {
    const { credential, credentialDeviceType, credentialBackedUp } =
      registrationInfo;

    const newAuthenticator = this.authenticatorRepository.create({
      credentialId: credential.id,
      credentialPublicKey: credential.publicKey,
      counter: credential.counter,
      user: user,
      webauthnUserId: user.webauthnId,
      deviceType: credentialDeviceType,
      backedUp: credentialBackedUp,
      transports: response.response.transports,
    });

    await this.authenticatorRepository.save(newAuthenticator);

    user.currentChallenge = null;
    await this.userRepository.save(user);

    return {
      verified,
      user: { id: user.id, email: user.email },
    };
  }

  throw new UnauthorizedException('Registration verification failed');
}


verifyRegistrationResponse
is what does the hard work in this code. It checks that the challenge matches the one you saved, that the response came from your origin and RP ID, and that the signature is valid. With 
requireUserVerification: true
it'll also reject the response if the UV flag isn't set. That flag is your proof that a fingerprint, face, or screen lock check took place.

If all goes well, you'll save the credential ID and the public key and then clear the challenge so it can't be reused.

How to Sign In with a Passkey on the Server

Sign-in works the same way: generate options, then verify the response.

Generate Authentication Options

async generateAuthenticationOptions(
    email: string,
): Promise {
  const user = await this.userRepository.findOne({ where: { email } });

  if (!user) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException('User not found');
  }

  const authenticators = await this.authenticatorRepository.find({
    where: { user: { id: user.id } },
  });

  if (authenticators.length === 0) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException(
      'No passkey registered for this account. Please sign up.',
    );
  }

  const options = await generateAuthenticationOptions({
    rpID: this.rpID,
    allowCredentials: authenticators.map((authenticator) => ({
      id: authenticator.credentialId,
      transports: authenticator.transports,
    })),
    userVerification: 'required',
  });

  // Save the current challenge
  user.currentChallenge = options.challenge;
  await this.userRepository.save(user);

  return options;
}


allowCredentials
lists the passkeys this user owns. The browser uses that list to find the right one on the device, and the 
transports
hint helps it decide whether to look locally, on a security key, or on a phone.

Verify the Authentication Response

async verifyAuthentication(
  email: string,
  response: AuthenticationResponseJSON,
) {
  const user = await this.userRepository.findOne({
    where: { email },
    select: ['id', 'email', 'currentChallenge'],
  });

  if (!user) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException('User not found');
  }

  const authenticator = await this.authenticatorRepository.findOne({
    where: { credentialId: response.id, user: { id: user.id } },
  });

  if (!authenticator) {
    throw new UnauthorizedException('Authenticator not found');
  }

  const verification = await verifyAuthenticationResponse({
    response,
    expectedChallenge: user.currentChallenge,
    expectedOrigin: this.origin,
    expectedRPID: this.rpID,
    credential: {
      id: authenticator.credentialId,
      publicKey: new Uint8Array(authenticator.credentialPublicKey),
      counter: Number(authenticator.counter),
      transports: authenticator.transports,
    },
    requireUserVerification: true,
  });

  const { verified } = verification;

  if (verified) {
    authenticator.counter = verification.authenticationInfo.newCounter;
    authenticator.backedUp =
      verification.authenticationInfo.credentialBackedUp;
    await this.authenticatorRepository.save(authenticator);

    user.currentChallenge = null;
    await this.userRepository.save(user);

    // Generate JWT token
    const payload = { sub: user.id, email: user.email };
    return {
      accessToken: this.jwtService.sign(payload),
      user: { id: user.id, email: user.email },
    };
  }

  throw new UnauthorizedException('Authentication verification failed');
}

The lookup uses both the credential ID and the user ID. Don't drop the user condition. I'll explain why in the security section.

The 

Number()
call around the counter is there because the 
pg
driver returns 
bigint
columns as strings. SimpleWebAuthn expects a number.

Once the signature has been verified, you increment the counter, clear the challenge, and issue a JWT. From that point on, the app treats the user exactly as it would any user who has signed in with a password. The only difference is that a password wasn't used.

How to Expose the Auth Endpoints

src/auth/auth.controller.ts

import { Controller, Post, Body, Get, Query, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from './guards/jwt-auth.guard';

@Controller('auth')
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly authService: AuthService) {}

  @Post('register/options')
  async getRegistrationOptions(
    @Body() body: { email: string },
  ): Promise {
    return this.authService.generateRegistrationOptions(body.email);
  }

  @Post('register/verify')
  async verifyRegistration(
    @Body() body: { email: string; response: any },
  ) {
    return this.authService.verifyRegistration(body.email, body.response);
  }

  @Post('login/options')
  async getAuthenticationOptions(
    @Body() body: { email: string },
  ): Promise {
    return this.authService.generateAuthenticationOptions(body.email);
  }

  @Post('login/verify')
  async verifyAuthentication(
    @Body() body: { email: string; response: any },
  ) {
    return this.authService.verifyAuthentication(body.email, body.response);
  }

  @Get('authenticators')
  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
  async getAuthenticators(@Query('email') email: string) {
    return this.authService.getAuthenticators(email);
  }
}

The 

response
body is typed as 
any
here because the service methods already declare the exact SimpleWebAuthn types they expect.

How to Protect Routes with a JWT

The last route uses

Next, create the Passport strategy that reads and validates the token in

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';

@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy) {
  constructor(private configService: ConfigService) {
    super({
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
      ignoreExpiration: false,
      secretOrKey: configService.get('JWT_SECRET'),
    });
  }

  async validate(payload: any) {
    return { userId: payload.sub, email: payload.email };
  }
}

Then create the guard in 

src/auth/guards/jwt-auth.guard.ts
. It wraps Passport's built-in guard and returns clearer error messages:
import {
  ExecutionContext,
  Injectable,
  UnauthorizedException,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { JsonWebTokenError, TokenExpiredError } from 'jsonwebtoken';

@Injectable()
export class JwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') {
  constructor() {
    super();
  }

  handleRequest(err: any, user: any, info: any) {
    if (info instanceof TokenExpiredError) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Token has expired');
    }

    if (info instanceof JsonWebTokenError) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid token');
    }

    if (err || !user) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Authentication failed');
    }

    return user;
  }

  // Optional: Override canActivate if you need custom logic before JWT validation
  async canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): Promise {
    const request = context.switchToHttp().getRequest();

    const authHeader = request.headers.authorization;
    if (!authHeader) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('No token provided');
    }

    const [type] = authHeader.split(' ');
    if (type !== 'Bearer') {
      throw new UnauthorizedException('Invalid token format');
    }
    return super.canActivate(context) as Promise;
  }
}

    TypeOrmModule.forFeature([User, Authenticator]),
    JwtModule.registerAsync({
      imports: [ConfigModule],
      useFactory: async (configService: ConfigService) => ({
        secret: configService.get('JWT_SECRET'),
        signOptions: {
          expiresIn: '1d',
        },
      }),
      inject: [ConfigService],
    }),
  ],
  controllers: [AuthController],
  providers: [AuthService, JwtStrategy],
})

How to Show Helpful Error Messages

When something goes wrong during a passkey ceremony, the browser throws a 

DOMException

name

Create 

client/src/services/passkey.ts

/* eslint-disable @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any */

// Turn errors from the browser's WebAuthn API and our backend into readable messages
export function getPasskeyErrorMessage(err: any, fallback: string): string {
  if (err?.response?.data?.message) {
    return err.response.data.message;
  }
  switch (err?.name) {
    case 'NotAllowedError':
      // User cancelled the fingerprint/face/screen-lock prompt, or it timed out
      return 'The passkey prompt was cancelled or timed out. Please try again.';
    case 'InvalidStateError':
      // A passkey for this account already exists on this authenticator
      return 'This device already has a passkey for this account. Please sign in instead.';
    case 'NotSupportedError':
      return 'This device does not support passkeys.';
    case 'SecurityError':
      return 'Passkeys are not allowed on this domain. Check the WebAuthn RP ID and origin settings.';
    default:
      return fallback;
  }
}


NotAllowedError
is the one you'll see most. It fires when the user closes the prompt, waits too long, or fails the biometric check. 
SecurityError
usually means your RP ID doesn't match the domain the page is running on, which is a configuration problem rather than a user problem.

Security Mistakes to Avoid

Passkeys are secure by design, but the server code around them still has to be right. I ran into each of the issues below while building this project. Some of them don't throw any errors, which is what makes them dangerous.

Encoding the Credential ID Twice

In recent versions of SimpleWebAuthn, including version 14 used here, 

credential.id
is already a base64url string. My first version of the code did this:
// Wrong: encodes an already-encoded string
credentialId: Buffer.from(credential.id).toString('base64url'),


Buffer.from
treats the string as UTF-8 text, so the result is a base64url encoding of a base64url string. Registration succeeds, but sign-in can never find the credential because the browser sends the original ID. Store 
credential.id
as it is.

Clearing the Challenge with 
undefined

Every challenge should be used only once. This line looks like it clears it:

user.currentChallenge = undefined;

But TypeORM skips 

undefined
properties when it saves an entity, so the old challenge stays in the database. Someone who captured a valid response could replay it. Set the value to 
null
instead, and make sure the column type allows it.

Looking Up a Credential Without Checking Its Owner

It's tempting to find the authenticator by credential ID alone:

// Wrong: any user's passkey matches
where: { credentialId: response.id }

But here's the problem: the attacker asks for sign-in options for your email, signs your challenge with their own passkey, and the server sees their passkey, validates the signature against their public key, and then issues a token for your account. Always include the user in the lookup as per the earlier example.

Letting Sign Up Add Passkeys to Existing Accounts

The registration endpoint is public. If it's going to add a passkey to an account that matches the email, then anyone who knows your email can register their own passkey and sign in as you.

Don't allow registration if the account already has a passkey. If you want people to be able to add more passkeys, then that can be a separate feature which requires them to be signed in.

Asking for Verification Without Requiring It

If you request 

userVerification: 'preferred'
, the device is allowed to skip the fingerprint or PIN check. If you then verify with 
requireUserVerification: true
, which is SimpleWebAuthn's default, users with those devices will get confusing failures. Pick 
'required'
on both sides so the options and the verification agree.

Where to Go From Here

The app you've built covers the fundamental passkey flows. But there are a couple of enhancements you could make if you wanted to go further.

Passkey autofill (also known as conditional UI) will cause the browser to suggest the saved passkey directly in the email field, just as it will suggest a saved password. SimpleWebAuthn supports this via the 

useBrowserAutofill
option of 
startAuthentication
.

Users will also want to add passkeys for their other devices and remove old ones. You'd build that as a pair of endpoints behind your JWT guard.

Finally, challenges should expire. A simple way to do this is to store a timestamp alongside 

currentChallenge
and then reject anything older than a few minutes. In a larger app, you'd probably store the challenges in a session or a cache (for example, Redis) rather than on the user record.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, you've built a complete passwordless authentication system using passkeys. You've got a full NestJS API that can generate WebAuthn challenges, verify the signed responses using SimpleWebAuthn, and store the public keys in PostgreSQL. You've also got a Next.js frontend that allows users to sign up and sign in using their fingerprint, their face, or their device's screen lock.

You've now learned how the challenge and signature flow works, why the user verification flag is important, and why the server can't decide which biometric method the user will see. You've also seen a number of rather subtle bugs that can result in a sign-in failure or even an account takeover, and how to avoid them.

Passwords aren't going away any time soon, but passkeys are already supported on pretty much every device that your users have. You now know how to add them to your own apps.

The full source code is available on GitHub. Go ahead and clone it, break it, and make it your own. If you found this tutorial useful in any way, then please do pass it on to someone who’s about to have the same question.

entries.content:
Data analysis might sound complicated when you first encounter it. You might imagine large databases, advanced mathematics, and complicated machine learning algorithms.

But many useful data analysis tasks start with something much simpler: loading a dataset, asking questions about it, and using Python to find the answers.

In this tutorial, you'll build a simple data analyzer using Python and pandas. You'll work with a fictional student performance dataset and learn how to load data, inspect it, calculate statistics, filter records, group information, and create a basic visualization.

By the end, you'll have a reusable foundation for analyzing many types of CSV datasets.

Prerequisites

Before following this tutorial, you should have a few basic Python skills and tools ready. You don't need advanced programming or data analysis experience, but you should be familiar with:

  • Python variables and basic data types, such as strings and numbers.
  • Importing libraries and calling functions.
  • Working with lists and basic operations on data.

If you're new to Python, consider learning these fundamentals before continuing. Here's an interactive Python course to get you started if you want to go deep.

Also, make sure you have the following installed:

  • Python: Python 3 or a compatible Python installation.
  • pandas: The Python library we'll use to load, filter, group, and analyze data.
  • Matplotlib: The library we'll use to create visualizations.
  • A code editor or IDE: Such as VS Code, PyCharm, or a simple text editor, along with access to a terminal.

You can install pandas and Matplotlib by running the following command in your terminal:

pip install pandas matplotlib

You'll also need a folder where you can save your Python script and the 

students.csv
dataset we'll create in this tutorial.

Once everything is ready, you can start analyzing data with Python!

What We'll Cover:

Setting Up Your Environment

Installing pandas

If you don't already have pandas installed, open your terminal and run:

pip install pandas matplotlib

We'll use pandas for data analysis and Matplotlib for a simple visualization.

You can verify the installation with:

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print(pd.__version__)

If Python prints a version number, you're ready to go.

Creating the Dataset

Creating a CSV File

We'll start by creating a file called 

students.csv
and adding some data.

The dataset we'll be working with here is fictional and contains 12 student records across grades 9 through 12. Each row represents one student, and each column describes a different attribute:

  • name
    : The student's first name.
  • grade
    : The student's current grade level in school.
  • study_hours
    : The number of hours the student studied.
  • attendance
    : The student's attendance percentage.
  • score
    : The student's test score, recorded on a 0–100 scale.

For example, Ava is in grade 9, studied for 4.5 hours, has 95% attendance, and received a test score of 82. These sample records let us explore questions such as whether study time is associated with test scores and how average scores compare across grade levels.

Because the data is fictional and small, any patterns we observe are only illustrative, and we shouldn't treat them as evidence about students in general.

But our data will give us enough information to perform several useful analyses. Here it is:

name,grade,study_hours,attendance,score
Ava,9,4.5,95,82
Liam,9,6.0,98,91
Sophia,10,3.5,89,76
Noah,10,7.0,99,94
Emma,11,5.5,93,88
Oliver,11,8.0,97,96
Mia,12,4.0,91,79
Ethan,12,6.5,96,90
Isabella,9,7.5,100,97
Lucas,10,2.5,85,68
Amelia,11,6.0,94,92
James,12,5.0,90,84

Loading the Dataset with Pandas

Reading the CSV File

Start your Python program by importing pandas:

import pandas as pd

Then load the CSV file:

data = pd.read_csv("students.csv")

The 

read_csv()
function reads the CSV file and converts it into a pandas DataFrame.

A DataFrame is a table-like data structure with rows and columns. You can think of it as a programmable spreadsheet.

Let's display the dataset:

print(data)

You should see the student records printed in your terminal.

Exploring the Data

Before analyzing a dataset, it's useful to understand what you're working with.

Viewing the First Rows

The 

head()
method displays the first five rows:
print(data.head())

You can also specify how many rows you want:

print(data.head(3))

Checking the Dataset Size

Use 

shape
to find the number of rows and columns:
print(data.shape)

The result will be:

(12, 5)

That means our dataset contains 12 rows and 5 columns.

Examining Column Names

You can view the column names with:

print(data.columns)

This is useful when you need to reference columns later in your program.

Checking Data Types

Use 

info()
to see information about each column:
data.info()

This helps you identify whether columns contain integers, decimal numbers, text, or other types of data.

Calculating Basic Statistics

Pandas makes it easy to calculate statistics without manually writing the mathematical formulas.

Finding the Average Score

We can calculate the average score using:

average_score = data["score"].mean()

print(f"Average score: {average_score:.2f}")

The 

mean()
method calculates the arithmetic average.

The 

:.2f
formatting tells Python to display the result with two decimal places.

Finding the Highest and Lowest Scores

Use 

max()
and 
min()
:
highest_score = data["score"].max()
lowest_score = data["score"].min()

print(f"Highest score: {highest_score}")
print(f"Lowest score: {lowest_score}")

You can also find the median:

median_score = data["score"].median()

print(f"Median score: {median_score}")

The median is the middle value when the scores are ordered.

Generating a Statistical Summary

Pandas also provides a convenient 

describe()
method:
print(data["score"].describe())

This produces statistics such as:

  • Count
  • Mean
  • Standard deviation
  • Minimum
  • 25th percentile
  • Median
  • 75th percentile
  • Maximum

You can generate a summary for all numerical columns:

print(data.describe())

This is often one of the first commands you'll use when exploring an unfamiliar dataset.

Filtering Data

One of the most useful features of pandas is the ability to select rows based on conditions.

Finding Students With High Scores

Suppose we want to find students who scored at least 90:

high_scores = data[data["score"] >= 90]

print(high_scores)

The expression:

data["score"] >= 90

creates a Boolean condition for every row. Pandas then keeps only the rows where that condition is 

True
.

Finding Students Who Study More Than Five Hours

We can perform the same operation using study time:

frequent_studiers = data[data["study_hours"] > 5]

print(frequent_studiers)

You can combine multiple conditions as well.

For example, suppose we want students who study more than five hours and have an attendance rate above 95 percent:

students = data[
    (data["study_hours"] > 5) &
    (data["attendance"] > 95)
]

print(students)

When combining conditions in pandas, use 

&
for AND and 
|
for OR. Each condition should be enclosed in parentheses.

Finding Specific Students

Using 
idxmax()

Sometimes you don't just want the highest value. You want to know which record contains it.

For example:

top_student_index = data["score"].idxmax()
top_student = data.loc[top_student_index]

print(top_student)


idxmax()
returns the index of the row containing the largest value.

We can do the same for study hours:

most_studious_index = data["study_hours"].idxmax()
most_studious_student = data.loc[most_studious_index]

print(most_studious_student)

This lets you connect a statistic back to the original record.

Grouping Data

Grouping becomes particularly useful when your dataset contains categories.

In our dataset, students belong to different grades.

Average Score by Grade

We can calculate the average score for each grade:

average_by_grade = data.groupby("grade")["score"].mean()

print(average_by_grade)

This tells us how the average score differs between grades.

We can make the output easier to read:

average_by_grade = (
    data.groupby("grade")["score"]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

print(average_by_grade)

Multiple Statistics

You can calculate several statistics at once:

grade_summary = data.groupby("grade")["score"].agg(
    ["mean", "min", "max", "count"]
)

print(grade_summary)

This produces a summary for each grade containing the average, minimum, maximum, and number of students.

Analyzing Study Time

We can also investigate the relationship between study hours and scores.

Calculating Correlation

Pandas provides a 

corr()
method:
correlation = data["study_hours"].corr(data["score"])

print(f"Correlation: {correlation:.2f}")

The correlation value generally ranges from -1 to 1.

A value closer to 1 indicates a stronger positive linear relationship, while a value closer to -1 indicates a stronger negative linear relationship. A value near 0 indicates little linear relationship.

However, correlation does not prove that one variable causes another. For example, if study hours and scores are correlated in this dataset, that doesn't prove that studying more directly caused higher scores.

Creating a Visualization

Numbers are useful, but visualizations can make patterns easier to recognize.

Creating a Scatter Plot

We'll create a scatter plot showing study hours and test scores:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.scatter(data["study_hours"], data["score"])

plt.xlabel("Study Hours")
plt.ylabel("Test Score")
plt.title("Study Hours vs. Test Scores")

plt.show()

Each point represents one student.

The x-axis represents study hours, while the y-axis represents test scores.

You may notice whether the points appear to generally move upward as study time increases.

This is what it should look like:

Creating a Bar Chart

We can also visualize the average score for each grade:

average_by_grade = data.groupby("grade")["score"].mean()

average_by_grade.plot(kind="bar")

plt.xlabel("Grade")
plt.ylabel("Average Score")
plt.title("Average Score by Grade")

plt.show()

A bar chart makes it easier to compare the averages between groups.

This is what the bar chart should look like:

Building the Complete Analyzer

Now let's combine the main ideas into one program.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load the dataset
data = pd.read_csv("students.csv")

# Basic information
print("Dataset shape:")
print(data.shape)

print("\nFirst five rows:")
print(data.head())

# Score statistics
average_score = data["score"].mean()
median_score = data["score"].median()
highest_score = data["score"].max()
lowest_score = data["score"].min()

print("\nScore Statistics")
print(f"Average: {average_score:.2f}")
print(f"Median: {median_score:.2f}")
print(f"Highest: {highest_score}")
print(f"Lowest: {lowest_score}")

# Students with scores of 90 or higher
high_scores = data[data["score"] >= 90]

print("\nStudents with scores of 90 or higher:")
print(high_scores[["name", "score"]])

# Average score by grade
average_by_grade = (
    data.groupby("grade")["score"]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

print("\nAverage Score by Grade:")
print(average_by_grade)

# Study hours and score correlation
correlation = data["study_hours"].corr(data["score"])

print(f"\nStudy Hours vs. Score Correlation: {correlation:.2f}")

# Scatter plot
plt.scatter(data["study_hours"], data["score"])

plt.xlabel("Study Hours")
plt.ylabel("Test Score")
plt.title("Study Hours vs. Test Scores")

plt.show()

This program now performs a small but complete data analysis workflow.

Making the Analyzer More Reusable

A useful next step is turning repeated operations into functions.

Creating an Analysis Function

Instead of writing everything directly in the main program, we can create a function:

def analyze_scores(data):
    average = data["score"].mean()
    median = data["score"].median()
    highest = data["score"].max()
    lowest = data["score"].min()

    print(f"Average score: {average:.2f}")
    print(f"Median score: {median:.2f}")
    print(f"Highest score: {highest}")
    print(f"Lowest score: {lowest}")

Then call it with:

analyze_scores(data)

This makes the code easier to reuse with another DataFrame.

Creating a Function for Top Students

We can also create a function that returns the highest-scoring students:

def get_top_students(data, minimum_score=90):
    return data[data["score"] >= minimum_score][
        ["name", "grade", "score"]
    ]

Now we can change the threshold whenever we want:

print(get_top_students(data, 95))

Functions like these become especially valuable when your analyzer grows.

Handling Missing Data

Real-world datasets are rarely as clean as our example. You may encounter missing values sometimes.

You can check for missing values with:

print(data.isnull().sum())

This tells you how many missing values exist in each column.

For example, you could remove rows containing missing values with:

clean_data = data.dropna()

Or, depending on the dataset and what the missing value means, you might replace missing values:

data["score"] = data["score"].fillna(data["score"].mean())

You should not automatically replace every missing value with an average. The appropriate approach depends on what the missing data represents and what you're trying to analyze.

Exporting Results

After analyzing a dataset, you may want to save your results.

For example:

average_by_grade.to_csv("average_scores_by_grade.csv")

You can also save filtered records:

high_scores.to_csv("high_scoring_students.csv", index=False)

The 

index=False
argument prevents pandas from adding the DataFrame's index as an extra column.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Forgetting to Import Libraries

Make sure the required libraries are imported:

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Otherwise, Python won't know what 

pd
or 
plt
means.

Using the Wrong Column Name

Column names must match your dataset.

For example, if the column is called 

study_hours
, this won't work:
data["study time"]

You can always check the actual column names with:

print(data.columns)

Confusing Correlation With Causation

A correlation can identify a relationship between variables, but it doesn't establish that one variable caused another.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as you work with larger and more complicated datasets.

Analyzing Before Understanding the Data

It's tempting to immediately calculate statistics. But first inspect the dataset.

Useful starting commands include:

data.head()
data.shape
data.info()
data.describe()
data.isnull().sum()

Understanding the structure and quality of your data helps prevent incorrect conclusions.

Where to Go From Here

The analyzer you've built is intentionally simple, but the same workflow can be applied to much larger datasets.

You could extend it to:

  • Analyze sales data
  • Track website traffic
  • Study survey responses
  • Analyze marketing campaigns
  • Examine sports statistics
  • Explore financial datasets
  • Track application or customer data

You could also add more advanced features such as interactive charts, command-line arguments, automated reports, or machine learning models.

For example, instead of hard-coding the CSV filename, you could let the user provide one:

filename = input("Enter the CSV filename: ")

data = pd.read_csv(filename)

print(data.head())

Now the same program can analyze different CSV files.

Final Thoughts

You don't need complicated algorithms to start working with data. With Python, pandas, and a relatively small dataset, you can already perform meaningful analysis.

In this tutorial, you learned how to:

  • Load CSV data with pandas
  • Explore a DataFrame
  • Calculate statistics
  • Filter rows
  • Find specific records
  • Group data
  • Calculate correlations
  • Create visualizations
  • Handle missing values
  • Export analysis results
  • Organize analysis with functions

The most important next step is to practice with different datasets. Once you're comfortable loading, exploring, cleaning, and analyzing data with pandas, you can start building much more sophisticated data-analysis projects.

Happy coding!

entries.content:
A noisy flight can make it difficult to enjoy a podcast or listen to music without turning up your volume super high.

Much of that disturbance comes from the steady rumble of the engines, which continues throughout the journey. Noise-cancelling headphones can reduce this background noise, making your listening experience more comfortable without requiring the surrounding environment to become any quieter.

This is possible because these headphones do more than physically cover your ears. They use microphones to capture surrounding sounds, electronic circuits to process the signals, and speakers to produce additional sound waves that counteract some of the incoming noise. The process happens continuously, allowing the headphones to respond to changes in the sound around you.

But how can one sound reduce another and how do headphones calculate the right signal quickly enough to make it work? The answer lies in the physics of sound waves and the real-time processing that brings this technology to life.

What We'll Cover:

First, Let's Understand What Sound Actually Is

Before exploring how headphones erase background noise, we first need to establish the basic physics of what sound actually is.

Sound isn't a physical object. Rather, it travels as a series of pressure variations moving through the air. When someone speaks or an engine rumbles, it pushes air molecules back and forth, creating invisible waves of high and low pressure.

So a microphone’s primary job is to convert these shifting pressure variations into an electrical signal, just as a headphone speaker converts an electrical signal back into moving air.

Because sound consists of these shifting pressure waves, two distinct sound waves can physically interact with each other when they meet in the air.

This fundamental interaction leads us directly to the principle of destructive interference. When two suitably matched sound waves overlap in perfectly opposite phases, their pressure variations can partially or even substantially cancel each other out.

For instance, if one wave produces a positive pressure variation (a peak) while another produces an equal negative variation (a trough) at the exact same moment, the combined variation can approach zero.

Mathematically, this relationship is quite simple:

ptotal(t)=pnoise(t)+panti-noise(t)

In this equation, p represents the sound pressure at a particular point in space and time. The crucial caveat, though, is that this cancellation is entirely local. So the waves don't disappear everywhere in the room. Instead, the noise cancellation works specifically by changing the sound pressure that reaches your individual ear.

How Do Headphones Create Anti-Noise?

To achieve destructive interference, the headphones must generate a sound wave specifically designed to oppose the incoming noise. We call this "anti-noise."

But it's not as simple as just playing a loud sound backward. The anti-noise signal needs to have an incredibly precise amplitude (loudness) and phase relationship with the original sound, precisely at the location of your eardrum.

Imagine an incoming sound wave that moves up and down like a roller coaster. The anti-noise must be an exact mirror image, moving down when the noise moves up and up when the noise moves down.

Simply having the opposite phase isn't enough, though. If the two waves don't arrive at the exact same time or if they have different amplitudes, you'll still hear residual noise. Because of this, consumer wearables don't generate a universal opposite wave for every sound in the entire room. Instead, they focus entirely on creating a very limited, tiny acoustic "quiet zone" right next to your ear canal.

Inside Noise Cancelling Headphones: The Real-time Process

So, how does a typical pair of ANC Headphones actually execute this in the real world? It all comes down to a continuously repeating signal processing pipeline.

First, external microphones capture the incoming ambient noise. In some advanced designs, internal microphones also measure the residual sound lingering near your ear.

Next, an internal digital controller processes this signal. It rapidly filters the microphone data and calculates the exact cancellation signal needed.

Then, the headphone speaker driver kicks into action, emitting a sound wave designed to oppose the incoming noise (the anti-noise).

Finally, the system continuously monitors and adjusts, constantly responding to your ever changing acoustic environment.

In this process, timing matters more than almost anything else. Sound takes time to travel and the digital system inside the headphones introduces processing and conversion delays. If the anti-noise arrives even a fraction of a millisecond too late, it can't cancel the original wave effectively.

The engineering challenge here is immense: the hardware must predict or respond to incoming noise while keeping its total delay exceptionally low. According to a 2018 study on the active feedforward noise control and signal tracking of headsets, minimizing processing delay is crucial for real-time applications because any lag immediately degrades the cancellation performance, especially for unpredictable sounds.

Feedforward, Feedback, and Hybrid ANC Explained

Not all noise-cancelling consumer wearables handle this processing loop the same way. Headphone designers can arrange their microphones and control systems in three primary configurations, depending on the desired performance and budget.

Feedforward ANC Listens Before the Noise Reaches Your Ear

This setup places the microphone on the outside of your ear cup. The controller uses this early information to prepare a cancellation signal.

The advantage here is getting a head start. The challenge, though, is that the system must perfectly estimate the time required for the sound to travel from the microphone to the ear, factoring in its own internal processing delays.

Feedback ANC Measures What Remains

An internal microphone sits inside the ear cup, capturing the sound right next to your ear, including the residual noise after cancellation. The controller uses this information to continuously correct its output.

Because it measures the result inside the cup, feedback alone has less opportunity to anticipate a sudden incoming sound before it reaches your ear.

Hybrid ANC Combines Both Approaches

Hybrid systems combine the best of both worlds. These systems use both external and internal microphone data to merge prediction with feedback-based correction.

As detailed in a 2019 study on reducing the effects of acoustic feedback in ANC systems, no single architecture is automatically best in every situation. Performance relies heavily on microphone placement, acoustic design, processing delays, and the specific type of noise you're trying to cancel.

The Algorithm Behind the Silence

Let's talk about the software side. An external microphone doesn't just pass a raw inverted signal directly to the speaker. The incoming audio must be carefully transformed using a digital filter to account for the headphone's own acoustic behaviour.

A digital filter uses the current and recent input samples to calculate an output signal. Its job isn't merely to invert every sample, but to output a signal that will successfully reduce noise after that signal has physically travelled through the headphone's speaker components and acoustic path.

To do this, many high-end headphones use adaptive algorithms. Filtered x Least Mean Squares (FxLMS) algorithm is one of the most established in active noise control.

The process is fascinating: the controller produces a cancellation signal, the internal microphone measures the residual noise (the "error"), and the algorithm uses that error data alongside a digital model of the speaker to ear acoustic path to tweak its filter coefficients. It's a continuous loop of measurement and refinement.

Not every pair of headphones uses FxLMS. Some rely on fixed, pre-trained filters, while others adapt actively. But as noted in the 2018 headset signal tracking research mentioned earlier, FxLMS based real-time control remains an incredibly effective standard for dynamic, on the fly adjustment.

Why Noise Cancellation Works Better on Some Sounds Than on Others

If you've worn these headphones, you've likely noticed a quirk: they easily erase an aircraft's engine rumble, but struggle to block out a crying baby or a nearby conversation. Why does this happen?

It all comes down to frequency and predictability. Low frequency sounds, such as steady ventilation noise or a bus engine, have long wavelengths and change relatively slowly over time. This gives the controller ample opportunity to estimate the waveform and generate an accurate cancellation signal.

Conversely, higher-frequency and sudden sounds are incredibly difficult to predict. A slamming door, a loud hand clap, or a sudden shout changes faster than the controller's processing loop can respond. The microphone, processing system, speaker, and acoustic path all have physical constraints that make high-frequency tracking incredibly difficult.

Beyond this, the direction from which the sound originates also plays a crucial role. A 2014 causality study on feedforward active noise control headsets highlighted how different noise arrival directions alter the delays involved, directly affecting how effectively the hardware can align the phases for destructive interference.

Why Passive Noise Isolation Still Matters

Because active cancellation has these inherent limitations, passive noise isolation remains incredibly important. While active cancellation relies on electronics, passive isolation relies entirely on physical barriers, like dense ear cups, tight acoustic seals, and foam ear tips to physically reduce the amount of sound entering the ear.

Unlike ANC, passive isolation doesn't generate an anti noise signal. But interestingly, the two methods are perfect companions. A strong physical seal naturally handles the high-frequency noises (like chatter and sudden claps) that are difficult for an ANC controller to cancel effectively. Think of standard earplugs for studying, for example: they're entirely passive, relying on foam or silicone to block sound. Active headphones rely on their physical design to do exactly that, leaving the heavy, low frequency lifting to the electronic ANC system.

What Happens When the Environment Changes?

The physics and signal processing sound flawless in a laboratory, but the real world is messy. As you go about your day, your acoustic environment is constantly shifting.

If you turn your head while walking, adjust an ear cup, or put on a pair of thick framed glasses, the acoustic path between the speaker and your eardrum changes. Even a slight break in the physical seal around your ear alters the sound reaching the microphone. When this happens, a cancellation signal that worked flawlessly a minute ago might suddenly become far less effective.

Can headphones adapt to this in real time? Yes, but to varying degrees. High end adaptive algorithms constantly adjust their filter coefficients using measurements of residual noise. Other models might seamlessly switch between a set of pre trained filters suited to different conditions.

A 2022 study on adaptive-gain algorithms for fixed filters demonstrated how modern headphones combine pre-trained data with adaptive weighting to handle these sudden environmental shifts smoothly. Real-time processing doesn't necessarily mean every part of the system is rewriting its code on the fly, but rather intelligently blending fixed strategies with live adjustments.

Does Noise Cancellation Remove All Sound?

It's time to correct a common misconception: active noise cancellation doesn't create a vacuum of total silence. Instead, it aggressively reduces unwanted low frequency sound. Human speech, sharp high-frequency noises, and sounds leaking through physical gaps will still easily reach your eardrum.

Some users occasionally report a feeling of "ear pressure" when they turn ANC on. This isn't the headphone blasting dangerous levels of air pressure into your skull. Rather, your brain is confused. It registers the sudden lack of low-frequency ambient noise as the sensation of pressure changes, much like an airplane ascending.

From a health perspective, ANC is quite beneficial, though it isn't a cure all. While it doesn't automatically protect your hearing from loud environments, it reduces background noise, which naturally encourages you to listen to your music at lower volumes. In fact, a 2012 study on noise canceling headphones and hearing hazards found that when people used ANC in background noise, their preferred listening levels were up to 4 dB lower compared to using ordinary earbuds.

While this isn't a guarantee for every listener, it shows how smart engineering can indirectly help protect our ears.

Conclusion

The next time you're sitting on a noisy train or an airplane, take a moment to appreciate the invisible tug of war happening right next to your ears. Your headphones aren't just a physical barrier against the outside world. They're actually actively measuring incoming noise, processing complex algorithms in milliseconds, and deploying targeted anti noise via a tiny speaker to reduce the original sound near your ear.

The sheer engineering required to pull this off is impressive. The internal controller must perfectly account for processing delays, acoustic behaviour, changing noise and the physical limits of its hardware. A quieter listening experience is the beautiful result of several systems working together seamlessly, bridging the gap between physics and computing in a device you can easily carry in your pocket or backpack.
